episodes.183034: A cutoff low produced multiple days of heavy rain. Hazards that resulted included gusty severe winds, flooding, funnel clouds, hail, and tree damage.
episodes.183851: An active pattern resulted in strong wind gusts in addition to isolated flash flooding to start the month of September.
episodes.184236: Clusters of slow moving thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall in a short period of time, leading to areas of flash flooding in Washington county and on St George Island.  Over 4 inches of rain was measured in Washington county and almost 7 inches of rain was measured on St George Island.
episodes.184241: A late summer pattern prevailed with scattered thunderstorms producing occasional gusty winds across the coastal waters with a waterspout also reported.
episodes.184777: Deep monsoon moisture moving north across northern Arizona and southern Utah brought heavy rain from thunderstorms.
episodes.185762: A deep southerly fetch of rich moisture up from the Gulf of California led to scattered to widespread heavy rainfall in Imperial and eastern Riverside counties during the afternoon of the 1st. Moisture values were well above normal for the time of year with precipitable water values analyzed around 2.0-2.2 inches. A Flash Flood Watch was issued for much of the region. Favorable dynamic and orographic forcing helped lead to strong updrafts and training of storms over certain terrain areas. Radar estimated rain rates were up to around 2-3 inches per hour with locally higher rates over shorter periods. There was a RAWS station in eastern Imperial County that measured right around 3 inches in 1 hour. These high rain rates led to areas of high rainfall accumulation, with many areas seeing at least 1 inch of rain and isolated areas up to 3.5-4.5 inches, radar estimated. This resulted in numerous reports of considerable flash flooding around the region. The hardest hit was the town of Niland and immediate surrounding area. A few inches of rain fell east of Niland leading to a canal being overcome with water and silt. This exacerbated the flooding and several inches of water flowed through the town and surrounding areas. The major impacts led to an emergency proclamation by the County of Imperial. In addition to the road closures, there were several swift water rescues across Imperial and Riverside Counties, both by land and air. One of the air rescues was completed by the San Diego US Coast Guard. On top of all the flooding, the heavy mass loading and strong updrafts resulted in strong to severe downburst winds, which caused a couple semi truck rollovers, downed many power poles, and generated dense  blowing dust.
episodes.185780: A deep closed low along the California coast and broad upper level ridging centered over the southern Plains promoted deep southerly flow across the Desert Southwest. This southerly flow promoted anomalous moisture advection into the area with PWATs upwards of 1.8-2 in the Lower Colorado River Valley area. Abundant moisture combined with CAPE upwards of 1,500-2,000 J/kg and a weak shortwave embedded in the flow allowed for efficient rain-producing thunderstorms to develop heading into the early afternoon hours on the 2nd. Several rain gages recorded over an inch of rainfall with these thunderstorms across southwest Arizona while radar estimates indicated locally heavier amounts in excess of 1.5 in some areas. As a result of these thunderstorms producing very heavy rainfall amounts in a short period of time, numerous instances of flash flooding occurred, particularly in the Yuma, Quartzsite, and Bouse areas. A couple of water rescues occurred, but no injuries were reported during this event.
episodes.185791: An upper level storm system coming from the Eastern Pacific interacted with monsoonal moisture on September 1, 2023. The interaction of these features led to the development of heavy rain and thunderstorms, which caused several instances of flooding in the Coachella Valley. Some instances of blowing dust were also observed.
episodes.186049: A push of monsoon moisture, which began in August, fueled thunderstorms over the Mojave Desert. Several produced flash flooding and high winds.
episodes.186050: A push of monsoon moisture, which began in August, fueled thunderstorms over the Mojave Desert and Owens Valley. Several produced flash flooding and high winds.
episodes.186051: A push of monsoon moisture, which began in August, fueled thunderstorms over the Mojave Desert. Several produced flash flooding, and one produced hail.
episodes.186106: Isolated gale-force wind gusts occurred in association with thunderstorms along a weak cold front drifting southwest over Florida Bay and portions of the Upper and Middle Florida Keys.
episodes.186142: An upper level low over northern California yielded a cooler,  wetter, and breezy pattern across the region through Labor Day weekend. Periods of light to moderate precipitation intermingled with isolated thunderstorms produced brief periods of heavy rainfall across the Sierra into northwest Nevada that caused some flash flooding and flooding concerns through the Labor weekend. Of particular concern was flooding in the playa area of the Black Rock Desert during the Burning Man festival.
episodes.186143: An upper level low over northern California yielded a cooler,  wetter, and breezy pattern across the region through Labor Day weekend. Periods of light to moderate precipitation intermingled with isolated thunderstorms produced brief periods of heavy rainfall across the Sierra into northwest Nevada that caused some flash flooding and flooding concerns through the Labor weekend. Of particular concern was flooding in the playa area of the Black Rock Desert during the Burning Man festival. A few isolated severe thunderstorms occurred across parts of the Basin and Range east of US-95 in Pershing, Churchill, and Mineral counties as well.
episodes.186160: A weak stalled boundary over the coastal waters triggered thunderstorms in some marine areas during the morning and early afternoon, causing some stronger wind gusts with the stronger storms. The activity tapered off throughout the day as the front washed out.
episodes.186213: A weak stalled boundary over the coastal waters triggered thunderstorms in some marine and land areas during the morning and early afternoon, causing some stronger wind gusts with the stronger storms. One particular cell took advantage of colliding boundaries and a moist airmass to produce a waterspout over the Mississippi River. The waterspout moved onshore and caused minor damage to buildings. The activity tapered off throughout the day as the front washed out.

Report of water flowing down Duncan Road and Sheep Creek Road, covering the westbound lanes in these areas.
ASOS station KNEW New Orleans Lakefront Airport measured a wind gust of 43 mph or 37 knots.

A weak tornado touched down just off the MS River in Kenner. It moved north along Minor Street and dissipated around Short Street. The windows of a police van were blown in with minor damage to the Kenner Fire Dept building. Tin roof was peeled off the theater and was blown south, a good indication of rotation. Other minor building damage was noted near the track. This determination was a combination of surveys from local emergency management, radar analysis and pictures and videos of a rotating funnel cloud in the area.
A trained spotter located 6.0 mi SSE Susanville, CA, reported a storm total rainfall amount of 1.45 inches.

Heavy rain fell across Coconino County. Some of the 24 hour rainfall amounts include (in inches): Arizona Snowbowl: 2.92, Bright Angel Point North Rim: 1.14, Four Springs RAWS: 1.13, Mable Canyon: 0.74, Tusayan: 0.73, and Jacob Lake 0.71.

Heavy rain fell across Yavapai County between September 2 and 3. Here are some 24 hour amounts (in inches) ending at noon on September 3: 11 miles SW of Prescott 1.28, 3 miles northwest of Camp Verde 1.25, 2 miles southwest of McGuireville 1.25,  and 2 miles southwest of Cottonwood 0.93.
Alamo Road was closed due to flooding.
Parker Dam Rd was washed out, and there was a rock slide just north of the Windmill Resort in Earp.

Bryce Canyon National Park Rangers reported rock slides and deep mud along the Navajo Loop trail as a result of heavy rain in the area. This resulted in damage to retaining walls along the trail, and as such, the temporary closure of the trail.

Images and videos showed a substantial amount of standing water along Madison Avenue near 23rd Street, impacting travel in the area. A car reportedly stalled in this intersection and had to be pushed out. Nearby in the intersection of 17th Street and 1st Avenue, video showed another stalled car having to be pulled out of the flooded roadway. No injuries were reported.
Virginia Drive was closed between 24th Street and 28th Street due to flooding. No damage or injuries were reported.

events.location: 9.74 NW Las Vegas N Air Term
events.narrative: Numerous streets and intersections were flooded, with water up to car windows in some cases. Several vehicles were stuck, including a city bus, and at least four water rescues were needed. One boy drowned.

A stream gauge along Bouse Wash at Plomosa Road rose above Action stage around 1415MST, making low water crossings along the wash impassable. The wash remained above Action stage into the morning hours on the 3rd. No damage or injuries were reported.

A video on social media showed a semi driving through a flooded low water crossing along SR 72 at Avenue 41 E with at least 6 inches of water flowing over the road. Timing was estimated from radar. No damage or injuries were reported.
Hacienda Road was flooded.
An image showed swift water flowing across 24th Street near South Avenue 5E, making the road impassable. No damage or injuries were reported.

As a result of heavy rain in the area, the East Fork Virgin - Springdale, guage recorded a  rapid rise in flow from its initial general flow level of around 68 CFS. An initial peak of 1228 CFS was observed at approximately 4:00 pm MST. The river then fell to 359 CFS at approximately 7:00 pm MST, before rising again to a secondary peak of 858 CFS at approximately 11:00 pm MST.

events.county: Coastal Waters From Oklaloosa-Walton County Line To Mexico Beach Out 20 Nm
events.narrative: A waterspout was observed and documented near St Andrews Bay.

As a result of heavy rain nearby, fairly substantial flash flooding was observed along Short Creek through the Hilldale area, with flood waters and debris crossing streets and overflowing culverts. A subsequent rise in flow from approximately 25 CFS to a peak of 1300 CFS was observed at the Fort Pearce Wash gauge downstream as the flood wave propegated.
A swift water rescue occurred after a single occupied vehicle attempted to drive through a flooded Bouse Wash low water crossing along Rabbit Lane near Stage Coach Road. No injuries were reported.
Part of Highway 62 was washed away near Highway 95, with over two dozen vehicles stuck.
Numerous washes along Highway 60 between mile markers 31-50 were flooded. Timing was estimated from radar. No damage or injuries were reported.
Flash flooding of Short Creek closed Hildale St.

Multiple washes were reported running in the Tacna area with one wash running at bankfull. Low water crossings east of Avenue 36 that run through the Gila River were reportedly closed due to flooding. During the event, a total of 2.04 of rain was observed within one hour in this area. No damage or injuries were reported.
The Lake Mead Blvd entrance to the Lake Mead National Recreation Area was closed due to water and debris across the road at Pabco Rd.
Ranch Road was closed due to flooding.
Water was flowing over Highway 95 at several locations.

Heavy rain from thunderstorms over southern Utah and far northern Arizona caused flash flooding in the Paria River. The river gauge on the Paria at Lees Ferry (Colorado River) showed a two foot rise between 415 PM and 645 PM.

Heavy rain over Agassiz Peak and the area between Agassiz Peak and Fremont Peak caused a flash flood on the southern side of Agassiz Peak. The Kachina Trail had two deep channels cut through it about 400 yards apart. Those channels were 10 to 12 feet deep and extended above and below the trail. Some of the rocks in the flow were 3 to 5 feet in diameter. The two channels joined and the debris, water, and mud flowed southwestward. Most of the debris formed an alluvial fan just uphill from Freidlein Prairie Road. Water and mud did flow across that road.
A motor home was stuck between two flooded areas on Goffs Rd near I-40.

Heavy rain over Agassiz Peak caused a flash flood on the northeastern side of the peak Peak into Locket Meadow. The water catchment in Snowslide Canyon was plugged with debris and damaged. One of the pump houses in the Inner Basin was damaged. The waterline that provides up to 30 percent of the water in Flagstaff during the summer was exposed and damaged in several locations. The access road around the water houses on Waterline Road was washed out.
